# RFC 3339 / RFC 9557 audit: Tempo timestamp consumers

**Scope:** I audited only the consumers: `timeutil.parse_timestamp` (RFC 3339), `timeutil.parse_ixdtf` (IXDTF, used by partner-feed ingest in `api.ingest`) and `client/parse.mjs` `parseTimestamp`/`parseSuffix` (IXDTF). The contract in `docs/API.md` sets these options: lower-case `t`/`z` accepted (`docs/API.md:43-44`), any number of fraction digits (`docs/API.md:38-39`), unknown elective tags ignored (`:49`), first duplicate wins (`:52`). It states no leap-second policy and no space separator.

**Evidence:** Static review only. No shell was available, so I did not run the scanner, the conformance vectors, `selfcheck` or `tests/test_timeutil.py`. Every "input → result" below comes from reading the code, not from running it.

**Summary:** 12 nonconformities, 1 deviation, 2 advisories, 5 review notes.

## Findings

| # | Severity | Ref | Target | Location | Finding | Evidence (traced) | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Nonconformity | 3339 §5.6 (`date-time = full-date "T" full-time`, `time-offset` required); 9557 §4.1 | consumer (ingest gate) | `timeutil.py:25`, `timeutil.py:107-108`, `timeutil.py:16`, reached through `timeutil.py:116` | The offset is optional in the regex. A missing offset is replaced with `default_tz` or `LOCAL_TZ`. `LOCAL_TZ` is the host's fixed offset, captured once at import, so it can also be wrong across DST. The result depends on the host time zone and can be the wrong instant. With IXDTF the zone suffix is also ignored when it computes the instant. | `"2026-04-02T18:00:00"` is accepted with the host offset. `"2026-04-02T18:00:00[Europe/Berlin]"` is accepted, and the instant is computed in the host zone, not Berlin. | Make the offset group mandatory and remove the `default_tz`/`LOCAL_TZ` fallback. |
| 2 | Nonconformity | 3339 §5.6 grammar | consumer | `timeutil.py:25` (`$`), `timeutil.py:99` | In Python, `$` also matches just before a trailing `\n`, so the string does not have to end where the grammar ends. `parse_ixdtf` inherits this through `head`. | `"2026-03-14T13:30:00Z\n"` is accepted. `"2026-03-14T13:30:00Z\n[Europe/Paris]"` is accepted. | Use `_TS_RE.fullmatch(text)` or end the pattern with `\Z`. |
| 3 | Nonconformity (also breaks 9557 §4.1 `suffix-values` grammar) | 9557 §3.3 (critical unprocessable MUST be erroneous; conflicting duplicates where one is critical MUST be erroneous) | consumer | `timeutil.py:127`, `timeutil.py:133-135`, `timeutil.py:27` | For key=value tags, the parser computes the critical flag and never uses it. `u-ca` values are not validated, and `_TAG_RE` accepts any value characters. | `"…Z[!u-ca=klingon]"` is accepted with calendar `klingon`. `"…Z[u-ca=hebrew][!u-ca=japanese]"` returns `hebrew` but should be an error. `"…Z[u-ca=he brew]"` is accepted. | Check values against `suffix-values` (`[A-Za-z0-9]+(-[A-Za-z0-9]+)*`). Check `u-ca` against the supported calendars and reject a critical unknown value. Keep `(value, critical)` per key and reject a conflicting duplicate if either copy is critical. |
| 4 | Nonconformity (wrong value) | 9557 §4.1 (`time-numoffset = sign time-hour ":" time-minute`) | consumer | `timeutil.py:27`, `timeutil.py:91`, `timeutil.py:139` | `_offset()` slices `[1:3]` and `[4:6]` without checking the format. Any key starting with `+` or `-` is treated as an offset zone. | `"[+0845]"` is read as +08:05, so `"2026-01-01T00:00:00+08:05[!+0845]"` passes the consistency check. `"[+08:45junk]"` is read as +08:45. | Match the zone against `^[+-]\d{2}:\d{2}$` (and the tz-name grammar) before interpreting it. |
| 5 | Nonconformity (too strict) | 9557 §4.1 (offset time zones allowed) | consumer (ingest) | `api.py:50` | `ingest` calls `ZoneInfo(start.zone)` on whatever `parse_ixdtf` returned. For a valid offset zone this raises `ZoneInfoNotFoundError` and the record fails ingest. | `"2026-04-02T18:00:00+08:45[+08:45]"`: the parse succeeds, then `ingest` raises. | Have `parse_ixdtf` return a resolved `tzinfo` (it already builds one at `timeutil.py:139`) and use that. |
| 6 | Nonconformity (too strict) | 3339 §5.6 (`time-second` 00-60, `date-fullyear` 4DIGIT), §5.7 | consumer | `timeutil.py:103-106` | Building a stdlib `datetime` rejects valid inputs: a leap second `:60`, and year 0000 (`MINYEAR` is 1). No profile restriction is documented. | `"2016-12-31T23:59:60Z"` raises `ValueError`. `"0000-01-01T00:00:00Z"` raises `ValueError`. | Validate `:60` against §5.7, then map it (for example to :59.999999 plus a flag) or document a "no leap second" profile. Also document or handle year 0000. |
| 7 | Nonconformity (too lenient, wrong value) | 3339 §5.6 grammar | consumer | `client/parse.mjs:13` | `STAMP_RE` has `$` but no `^`, so `exec` matches a valid-looking tail anywhere in the string. | `"garbage2026-03-14T09:30:00Z"` is accepted. `"12026-03-14T09:30:00Z"` is accepted as year 2026. | Add `'^' +` at the start of the pattern. |
| 8 | Nonconformity (too strict) | 3339 §5.6 NOTE (`T`/`Z` may be lower case); ABNF is case-insensitive | consumer | `client/parse.mjs:10`, `client/parse.mjs:11`, `client/parse.mjs:20` | Only upper-case `T` and `Z` are accepted. This contradicts `docs/API.md:43-44`. | `"1985-04-12t23:20:50.52z"` throws "invalid timestamp". The Python parser accepts it (`tests/test_timeutil.py:41-44`). | Use `[Tt]` and `[Zz]`, and compare case-insensitively in `parseOffset` and at line 89. |
| 9 | Nonconformity (wrong instant) | 3339 §5.7 (day must fit month and year) | consumer | `client/parse.mjs:17`, `client/parse.mjs:68`, `client/parse.mjs:77` | Every month is capped at day 31. `Date.UTC` then rolls invalid dates into the next month. | `"2023-02-30T10:00:00Z"` returns `iso: "2023-03-02T10:00:00.000Z"`. `"2025-04-31T…"` gives May 1. | Check against the actual days in the month (with leap-year rules), or compare the `Date.UTC` result's fields back to the input. |
| 10 | Nonconformity (too lenient) | 3339 §5.7 (`:60` only at a month end in which a leap second occurs, offset-adjusted) | consumer | `client/parse.mjs:71` | `second === 60` is accepted at any time of day and any date. | `"2026-03-14T09:30:60Z"` is accepted with `leapSecond: true`. | Allow `:60` only when the UTC-adjusted time is 23:59 on the last day of a month. Choose a month policy (see review notes). |
| 11 | Nonconformity (wrong instant) | 3339 §5.6 (`date-fullyear` 0000-9999) | consumer | `client/parse.mjs:77` | `Date.UTC` maps years 0–99 to 1900–1999. | `"0050-06-01T00:00:00Z"` returns `iso: "1950-06-01T00:00:00.000Z"`. | Build the date with `new Date(0)` plus `setUTCFullYear(year, month-1, day)`, or use `Temporal.Instant.from`. |
| 12 | Nonconformity | 9557 §3.3 (critical unknown key/value MUST be erroneous; first occurrence of a repeated key wins; critical conflict is erroneous) | consumer | `client/parse.mjs:33-34`, `client/parse.mjs:50`, `client/parse.mjs:51` | Unknown keys are skipped (`continue`) even when marked critical. Repeated keys overwrite, so the last one wins. Critical `u-ca` values are not validated. This contradicts `docs/API.md:50-52`. | `"…Z[!x-foo=bar]"` is accepted. `"…Z[u-ca=chinese][u-ca=japanese]"` gives `calendar: "japanese"` (should be `chinese`). `"…Z[!u-ca=klingon]"` is accepted. | For an unknown key: throw if critical, otherwise skip. Keep only the first value per key and throw on a conflict if any copy is critical. Validate calendar identifiers when the tag is critical. |
| 13 | Deviation (false contract, reported once) | 3339 §5.6; 9557 §3.3 | consumer contract | `docs/API.md:19-21`, `:43-44`, `:49`, `:52` | The documented contract does not match the consumers: (a) it tells clients to accept "any ISO 8601" including the compact `20260314T133000Z`, which is not RFC 3339, and neither parser accepts it; (b) lower-case is rejected by the JS parser (#8); (c) "unknown elective tags are ignored", but Python rejects them (#A1); (d) "first occurrence is used", but JS uses the last (#12). | See the linked rows. | Restrict the contract to RFC 3339 and RFC 9557 (drop the compact form), then align both parsers with it. |
| A1 | Advisory | 9557 §3.3 (unknown elective key: may be ignored) | consumer | `timeutil.py:133-134` | Every unknown key is rejected, whether elective or critical, so the elective/critical distinction is lost. This also breaks partner feeds that add harmless tags. | `"2026-04-02T18:00:00+02:00[Europe/Berlin][x-src=feed]"` raises "unsupported suffix key". | Skip unknown elective keys. Reject unknown critical keys and `_`-prefixed experimental keys. |
| A2 | Advisory | 9557 §2 (`Z` = offset unknown vs `+00:00` = UTC preferred) | consumer → re-emit | `timeutil.py:88-89`, `timeutil.py:94`, `api.py:50,54` (then `format_ixdtf`); `client/parse.mjs:20,98` | Both consumers turn `Z`, `-00:00` and `+00:00` into the same zero offset. On ingest, a `Z` input with no suffix is re-emitted as `+00:00[UTC]`, which states a local context the partner never gave. | `ingest({"start": "2026-04-02T16:00:00Z", …})` gives a `start` of `"2026-04-02T16:00:00+00:00[UTC]"`. | Keep an `offset_known` flag in `Stamp` and in the JS result, and emit `Z` when the offset is unknown. |

## Review notes
- **Sub-minute (LMT) zone offsets** (`timeutil.py:147`, `client/parse.mjs:59,90`): the consistency check compares exact offsets. Before a zone adopted standard time its offset often had seconds (for example Paris before 1911 was +00:09:21), which `time-numoffset` cannot express. So any historical timestamp with a critical zone is always rejected. RFC 9557 leaves this open. Rounding to the nearest minute is a reasonable tolerance.
- **Leap-second representation** in JS (`client/parse.mjs:77,99`): mapping `:60` to `:59` and setting `leapSecond` is an acceptable choice once #10 is fixed. For the month rule I would use the Appendix D reading (end of March, June, September or December from 1972), or the real IERS table.
- **Temporal dependency** (`client/parse.mjs:58`): this needs a global `Temporal`. Without it, the `catch` at line 85 rejects every critical zone and silently drops elective ones. That is conformant (the zone cannot be evaluated), but it quietly degrades behaviour, so check the target runtimes.
- **Handled correctly:** `Z`/`-00:00` with a critical zone skips the consistency check (`timeutil.py:145`, `client/parse.mjs:89`). Unknown elective zones are dropped and unknown critical zones rejected. The zone is required to come first. Experimental `_` keys are rejected (`client/parse.mjs:49`; Python rejects them through its allowlist). Offset ranges are checked. Fractions are truncated to µs/ms. Python validates impossible dates. Python's first-wins for elective duplicates is right (`timeutil.py:135`).
- **Tz-name grammar:** neither parser checks it directly. They rely on `ZoneInfo` or Temporal to reject bad names. Note that `ZoneInfo` lookups follow the filesystem, so on case-insensitive filesystems like macOS they may accept wrong-case names.

## Not run / not applicable
- `rfcdt.py scan`, `run_vectors.py` (310 vectors), `rfcdt.py selfcheck` and the unit tests were not run because no shell was available. None of the vector buckets are graded from tool output, and I make no clean-result claims.
- **Out of scope (producers and schema), not graded, but worth a follow-up:**
  - `format_utc` (`timeutil.py:51`, used at `api.py:33`) labels the local wall time with `Z`, which gives the wrong instant.
  - `%z` gives `-0400` with no colon (`timeutil.py:13,56`).
  - `format_reminder` drops the seconds (`timeutil.py:61`, and the test at `tests/test_timeutil.py:32` asserts that).
  - `created_at` is naive, so it has no offset (`api.py:25,36`).
  - `all_day_date` is a date but the schema says `format: date-time` (`schema/event.schema.json:50`).
  - `format_epoch` emits `+00:00` for an unknown offset (`timeutil.py:66`).
  - `zone_label` produces `[UTC+05:30]` for fixed offsets (`timeutil.py:70`).
  - The `start` pattern in the schema is `\[.+\]` (`schema/event.schema.json:21`).
  - Given all of the above, the "CI guarantees well-formed" claim in `docs/API.md:13-15` is false.

## Assumptions
- `parse_ixdtf` is treated as an input gate because it handles partner-feed ingest (`timeutil.py:3-4`, `docs/API.md:58-59`), and `parse_timestamp` because it claims RFC 3339. That is why leniency is graded as a Nonconformity.
- The only supported calendar is `u-ca` (`KNOWN_SUFFIX_KEYS` and `KNOWN_KEYS`).
- The system tz database is available to `zoneinfo`, and Temporal is available to the client.

## Reproduction
This is a static trace against the files as they are in the working tree, with no versions probed. To confirm, write a small adapter for each parser (read a string on stdin, print `{"ok": …, "fields": …}`) and run:

`python3 ~/.claude/skills/rfc3339-ixdtf/scripts/run_vectors.py --target "<adapter>" --target-kind both --target-has-tzdata yes --tz-matrix UTC,America/St_Johns,Asia/Kathmandu --report md`

The `--tz-matrix` option will show the host-time-zone dependence in #1. Record the output of `rfcdt.py selfcheck` alongside the results.

I checked all three flagged items against the RFC text: **none of them violates RFC 3339 or RFC 9557.** Each one is either explicitly allowed or required by the RFCs. While checking them I found other timestamp problems in the same files that are real violations. They're in the report below.

## The three flagged items

**(1) `format_instant` always writes three fractional digits and `Z`: not a violation.**
- The grammar allows any number of fraction digits (`time-secfrac = "." 1*DIGIT`, §5.6). The §5.6 NOTE says a specification may restrict the format further as long as the output stays inside the grammar, and `docs/API.md:34-39` states this millisecond restriction.
- Cutting off extra digits rather than rounding is fine.
- `Z` is also correct. Under RFC 9557 §2, `Z` means "UTC is known, local offset unknown", which fits a server receipt time. Sample output: `2026-03-14T13:30:05.987Z` (from `tests/test_timeutil.py:17`), which is valid.
- Severity: none.

**(2) `timeutil` accepts lower-case `t` and `z`: not a violation.**
- The §5.6 NOTE says `T` and `Z` "may alternatively be lower case". ABNF strings are case-insensitive, so `1985-04-12t23:20:50.52z` is valid input and rejecting it would be too strict.
- The code handles it consistently: `_TS_RE` at `timeutil.py:22,25`, `_offset` at `:88`, and the `"Zz"` test at `:145`.
- One small related point: `client/parse.mjs:10-11` accepts upper case only. The §5.6 NOTE allows that restriction, but it contradicts `docs/API.md:43-44` ("Parsers accept lower-case"). That's a documentation problem, folded into finding 13.

**(3) Both parsers skip the critical-zone consistency check for `Z` and `-00:00`: not a violation, and required.**
- RFC 9557 §3.4 and the §2 update say `Z` or `-00:00` assert no local offset. So `2022-07-08T00:14:07Z[!Europe/London]` is consistent and must not be rejected. Running the check here would be the error.
- Both parsers still reject an explicit mismatch such as `+00:00[!Europe/London]` (`timeutil.py:145-148`, `parse.mjs:89-91`, test at `tests/test_timeutil.py:56-62`).
- One catch: in `timeutil`, a date-time with no offset at all counts as "offset known" and gets compared using the host's local zone. The root cause is finding 6.

# RFC 3339 / RFC 9557 adherence: Tempo timestamp contract

**Scope:** the schema (`schema/event.schema.json`) and the contract docs (`docs/API.md`). The contract claims two profiles: `start` is IXDTF (RFC 9557) and the other fields are RFC 3339 `date-time`. Options it declares:
- Generators emit upper-case `T`/`Z` and parsers accept `t`/`z` (API.md:43-44).
- `received_at` has exactly 3 fraction digits and ends in `Z` (API.md:36-37).
- Clients accept fractions of any length (API.md:38-39).
- `start` must carry a zone suffix (schema:19-21).
- Suffix rules are at API.md:46-54.

**Evidence:** I reviewed everything statically. No shell was available, so I didn't run `rfcdt.py scan`, the vector runner or `selfcheck`. To check the contract's claims, I worked out producer output by hand from `api.py` and `timeutil.py`. I did not execute those outputs; they are marked "traced" below.

**Summary:** 5 nonconformities, 2 deviations, 2 advisories, 7 review notes. A further 6 implementation defects are listed after the table but not counted.

## Findings

| # | Severity | Check ID | Ref | Target | Location | Finding | Evidence | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Nonconformity** | R3339-5.6-03/04/05/06/07/09/16, R9557-4.1-01/02, R9557-3.2-01 (schema side), R9557-3.3-04 | 3339 §5.6; 9557 §3.1, §4.1 | schema | schema/event.schema.json:21 (claim at :19) | The `start` pattern is the only check on `start` (it has no `format`). It uses `[0-9]{2}` with no range limits, and `\[.+\]$` accepts any text in brackets. The suffix grammar is not enforced: it doesn't require the zone first, doesn't limit key characters (lower case only), doesn't validate the `!` flag, and doesn't stop trailing text. It also accepts a string with only a calendar tag and no zone, although API.md:25 says the zone is always there. | These all match the pattern: `2026-13-45T25:61:99+99:99[x]`, `…+05:30[UTC+05:30]` (`:` is not allowed in `time-zone-part`), `…Z[U-CA=hebrew]` (upper-case key), `…Z[_foo=bar]` (experimental key), `…Z[Europe/Paris] junk]`, `…-04:00[u-ca=hebrew]` (no zone), `…Z[!!x]`. | Put a strict RFC 3339 core in the pattern (month `0[1-9]\|1[0-2]`, hour `[01][0-9]\|2[0-3]`, …, offset `[+-]([01][0-9]\|2[0-3]):[0-5][0-9]`). Then use `\[!?(zone-name\|[+-]HH:MM)\](\[!?[a-z][a-z0-9-]*=[A-Za-z0-9]+(-[A-Za-z0-9]+)*\])*$`, where the name parts follow §4.1 `time-zone-part`. Add `"not":{"pattern":"\n"}` because Python and .NET let `$` match before a trailing newline. |

Finding #1 means the schema lets it through. | evt_0002 (traced): `2026-05-04T10:00:00+05:30[UTC+05:30]` | Make the suffix optional for events with no IANA zone (§3.3: suffixes are optional). ### Where the code breaks the contract (evidence only, not counted)
These fall outside the scope you gave me (schema and docs), but they show where rows of the contract are broken:
- **Wrong time in `start_utc`.** timeutil.py:51 adds a literal `Z` to local wall time without converting to UTC. evt_0001 gives `2026-03-14T09:30:00Z` where it should be `13:30:00Z`. That breaks API.md:26 ("the same instant as `start`"). The string is well-formed, so no schema can catch it. This is the most serious defect in the service.
- **Offsets without a colon.** timeutil.py:13 and :56 use `%z`, which writes `-0400`.
- **Seconds dropped.** timeutil.py:61 leaves the seconds out of `reminder_at`.
- **No offset on `created_at`.** api.py:25 uses naive `datetime.now`, so `created_at` has no offset.
- **Ingest assumes host time.** On the ingest side (API.md:58-59), timeutil.py:25 makes the offset optional and timeutil.py:108 then assumes host-local time. `2026-04-02T18:00:00[Europe/Berlin]` is accepted.
- **Unknown tags rejected.** timeutil.py:133-134 rejects every unknown tag, which contradicts API.md:49. This is an Advisory under rule 4.

## Review notes
- **Case, schema:21 vs API.md:43-44.** The `start` pattern accepts only upper-case `T`/`Z`. §5.6 NOTE lets a producer profile restrict case, so this is fine for checking server output. But clients that reuse the schema to check input would be too strict compared with API.md:44. Say which use the schema is for.
- **Required suffix, schema:21.** RFC 9557 §3.3 lets an application require suffix tags, so requiring one is a valid profile choice in itself. Finding #2 is only about how the requirement is met.
- **`[Area/City]`, API.md:25.** This wording is narrower than the RFC 9557 grammar and the tz database. It leaves out `UTC`, `Etc/GMT+5`, three-part names like `America/Argentina/Buenos_Aires`, and offset zones. I read it as descriptive, not as a restriction.
- **`Z` in `start`, API.md:25 vs schema:21.** The docs say "numeric offset" but the pattern allows `Z`. `Z[zone]` is valid and means the local offset is unknown (9557 §3.4 Fig. 2). Pick one.
- **API.md:50-54.** It says unprocessable critical *tags* are errors, but not that an unknown critical *zone name* is also an error (9557 §3.3/§4.1). The code handles that case (timeutil.py:141-142). The rule "with `Z` there is no disagreement" should also cover `-00:00` (9557 §2); timeutil.py:145 already does.
- **API.md:48.** "Zone suffix comes first" is correct (§4.1: `suffix = [time-zone] *suffix-tag`).
- **Not stated anywhere:** the leap-second policy (whether `:60` is accepted and on which dates), and the fraction precision for fields other than `received_at`. RFC 3339 allows these to vary, so this isn't a defect, but clients need to know.

## Not run / not applicable
- `rfcdt.py scan`, `run_vectors.py`, `rfcdt.py check` and `selfcheck` were not run because no shell was available. So there are no vector pass rates and no tool-verified producer samples. All producer strings above are traced by hand from the source.
- I did not audit the client (`client/parse.mjs`) because it was out of scope.
- I found no CI or validator configuration in the repo (the only files are `api.py`, `timeutil.py`, `tests/`, `client/`, `schema/` and `docs/`), so I had no configured validator to test against.

## Assumptions
- The schema is checked with a draft 2020-12 validator and default settings (format is annotation only), since the repo sets up nothing else.
- Patterns follow ECMA-262 semantics, as JSON Schema specifies. The trailing-newline problem only applies on Python and .NET validators.
- tz data: New York on 2026-03-14 is UTC−04:00 (DST starts 2026-03-08).
